title: Forms, chains, and Stokes' theorem
one_line_summary: Rebuilds integration on the Part V machinery: every multiple integral becomes the pairing of a p-form with the p-dimensional region (a chain) it is evaluated on, the boundary operator is introduced with the rule that boundaries have no boundary, and the generalized Stokes theorem, the integral of d(Omega) over C equals the integral of Omega over the boundary of C, is stated as the single statement behind the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green, Kelvin-Stokes and Gauss.
role_in_book: Final chapter of Part V (Geometry); a margin box calls it the logical end point of that part and says it can be skipped on a first pass. It gathers the p-forms, p-vectors and tube/cell pictures of Chapter 32, the exterior derivative and dd = 0 of Chapter 33, and the volume forms and Hodge duals of Chapter 37, and turns them into a theory of integration. It also explains after the fact where the Jacobian of Section 5.4 comes from. Its main customer is Chapter 43, where Stokes' theorem expresses charge conservation and the geometric meaning of the Bianchi identity, and Exercise 38.4 previews holonomy (rotation of a transported vector by enclosed curvature) in a two-dimensional setting.

assumed_background.topic: Fundamental theorem of calculus and Riemann sums
Vector-calculus integral theorems (divergence theorem, Stokes curl theorem, Green's theorem), line and flux integrals
Jacobian determinant for changing variables in multiple integrals
Determinants written with the Levi-Civita symbol
p-forms, wedge product, bivectors and p-vectors, the sheet/tube/cell pictures and the ordered-index pairing of a p-form with a p-vector
Exterior derivative and its nilpotency dd = 0
Hodge star, volume forms and the 3-volume 1-form d sigma
Metric determinant and the invariant volume element sqrt|g|
Conservative forces and work as a line integral
Flux and charge conservation in electromagnetism
Simply connected spaces, holes in a domain (informal topology)
Connection coefficients in an orthonormal frame and parallel transport (for Exercise 38.4)

learning_objectives: Reader can explain with a telescoping sum why integrating a derivative over an interval leaves only the end values, with a plus sign at the far end and a minus sign at the near end.
Reader can rewrite a work integral as the integral of a 1-form and a flux integral as the integral of a 2-form, and say what each integral counts in the sheet, tube and cell pictures.
Reader can derive the two-dimensional Jacobian determinant by expanding a wedge of two transformed basis 1-forms and using antisymmetry.
Reader can evaluate the integral of an n-form over a parametrized n-dimensional region as the parameter integral of the pairing between the form and the wedge of the tangent vectors dP/dlambda^i.
Reader can write the flat-spacetime volume 4-form and the 3-forms dSigma_mu, and interpret J^mu dSigma_mu as a flux 3-form ready to be integrated over a hypersurface.
Reader can define chains, cycles and boundaries, apply the boundary operator to discs, cylinders, curves and spheres, and argue that the boundary of a boundary vanishes.
Reader can state the generalized Stokes theorem with its boundary-orientation rule and describe the duality in which d raises form degree while the boundary operator lowers chain dimension.
Reader can recover the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, the Kelvin-Stokes theorem and the divergence theorem as special cases of the generalized theorem.
Reader can distinguish closed from exact forms, quote the Poincaré lemma, and show that the vortex 1-form on the punctured plane is closed but not exact.
Reader can use Green's theorem on the unit sphere to show that parallel transport round a closed loop rotates a vector by an angle equal to the enclosed area.

teaching_approach.summary: A consolidation chapter. It opens with the familiar family of vector-calculus integral theorems, isolates what they share (derivative integrated inside equals the function summed with signs on the edge), announces the one-line generalization at once, and then rebuilds integration out of Part V objects so that the one-liner can be read literally. The integrand is re-identified as a form that already contains its differentials; the domain is a parametrized region whose infinitesimal piece is a wedge of tangent vectors; the integral is their pairing, which makes the Jacobian automatic rather than a rule. Chains and the boundary operator are introduced by pictures and short lists rather than by algebraic topology, Stokes' theorem is stated without proof, and the theorem is exercised on volume and area elements and on recovering the divergence theorem. Topological subtleties (closed versus exact, cycles that are not boundaries) and the holonomy application live in margin notes and exercises.
narrative_arc: Frame: epigraph on integrating infinitesimals and the long-s origin of the integral sign present integration as summation.
Motivating pattern: the fundamental theorem of calculus depends only on signed end values; slicing the interval into a telescoping sum shows why interior pieces cancel.

Extend by analogy to three dimensions (volume integral of a gradient equals a surface term, hence the divergence theorem) and to two dimensions (area integral of gradient-cross-area equals minus a loop integral, hence the curl theorem); note the family resemblance and the mismatched appearances.
Announce the destination immediately: the integral of dOmega over C equals the integral of Omega over the boundary of C (eqn 38.7).
Upgrade notation: a work integral is the integral of a 1-form and a flux integral is the integral of a 2-form; defend writing an integral with no explicit dx.
Promise the dual picture: integrands are forms, domains are chains, and their pairing is a number (eqn 38.12).
Geometric meaning: a line integral counts sheets crossed, a surface integral counts tubes pierced, a volume integral counts cells enclosed.
First payoff: the Jacobian of a change of variables drops out of wedge-product antisymmetry (Example 38.1).
Anatomy of the integrand: a function times a wedge of coordinate 1-forms; the spacetime volume 4-form, the 3-forms dSigma_mu and the flux 3-form J^mu dSigma_mu (Example 38.2).

Anatomy of the domain: an infinitesimal parallelepiped built from tangent vectors to a parametrized surface; the integral defined as the parameter integral of the pairing; the pairing of coordinate wedges with tangent wedges is the Jacobian (eqns 38.30-38.32).
Sanity check: the integral of df along a curve returns the end-value difference (Example 38.3).
Domains as dual objects: define boundary, list examples and draw them with the boundary operator (Example 38.4, Fig. 38.1).
Chains C_n, the dimension-lowering boundary operator, cycles Z_n, boundaries B_n, and the conclusion that applying the boundary operator twice gives zero.

Mirror operator: the exterior derivative raises degree; recompute curl-like and divergence-like components in 3D and verify dd = 0 (Example 38.5); present dd = 0 as the dual of the double-boundary rule; closed/exact forms and the Poincaré lemma in a margin note.
State Stokes' theorem with its boundary orientation rule; decline to prove it and point to Needham and Spivak.

Exercise the theorem: metric volume integrals with sqrt(g) (Example 38.6), surface integrals via an area 2-form (Example 38.7), recovery of the endpoint, surface-edge and volume-surface theorems and in detail the divergence theorem (Example 38.8, Fig. 38.2).
Forward look to charge conservation and curvature constraints in Part VI; exercises on Kelvin-Stokes, the sphere, the vortex form, and holonomy on the sphere.
signature_moves: Stating the final theorem (eqn 38.7) near the start so every later definition visibly serves one goal.
Openly defending the unconventional notation of an integral without a trailing differential, by folding the differentials into the form.
Reusing the Chapter 32 pictures of forms (planes, tubes, cells) to turn integration into counting how many pieces of the form the domain meets.
Presenting the Jacobian as a by-product that certifies the forms formalism, rather than as a correction factor to memorize.
Defining the integral as a literal instance of the form-vector pairing, so that 'domains are dual to integrands' feels like the old statement that 1-forms eat vectors.
Pictorial boundary algebra (Fig. 38.1): a column of shapes with the boundary operator applied, empty boundaries drawn as a dissolving puff borrowed from Douglas Adams.
Placing the two operators side by side (d raises degree, boundary lowers dimension; dd = 0 mirrors the double-boundary rule) so that Stokes reads as an adjointness statement.
Keeping rigorous topology (simplicial complexes, homology, the Poincaré lemma) in margin notes and exercises so the main line stays short.
Closing the exercise set with a relativity-flavoured payoff: Stokes' theorem turns parallel transport round a loop on a sphere into a rotation by the enclosed area.

sections.title: Integration
sections.summary: Starts from the fundamental theorem of calculus and asks why only the end values survive and why they carry opposite signs; slicing the interval gives a telescoping sum. The same pattern is pushed to three dimensions (a gradient integrated over a volume equals the function integrated over the oriented bounding surface, which yields the divergence theorem) and to two dimensions (a gradient-cross-area integral equals minus a loop integral, which yields the curl theorem). The three results clearly share one idea but look different, so the chapter announces the unifying statement and upgrades notation: work integrals become integrals of 1-forms, flux integrals become integrals of 2-forms written with wedges, and integrands (forms) are said to be dual to domains (chains). A margin box marks the chapter as optional on first reading and needed for Chapter 43; a margin note restricts attention to flat space.
key_moves: Discretize the integral of df/dx into differences f(x_{i+1}) - f(x_i); adjacent terms cancel leaving f(b) - f(a).
Interpret the sign flip at the two ends as the orientation of the boundary; in 3D the outward surface element plays that role.
Set f = a^j in the vector gradient theorem and sum over j to get the divergence theorem.
Write the 2D analogue with a cross product, take its i-th component with epsilon_{ikm}, set f = a^j and contract i with j to get the curl theorem.
Announce the target eqn 38.7 before building any machinery.
Identify F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz as a 1-form and G_x dy^dz + ... as a 2-form, so both integrals become integral of a form over a domain.
State the pairing slogan: (form, chain) gives a number, namely the multiple integral.

sections.title: Integrating over forms
sections.summary: Recalls the pictures of forms of each degree (a function; stacked planes; a lattice of tubes; an array of cells) and reads each integral as a count: a curve integral of a 1-form counts the planes the curve crosses, a surface integral of a 2-form counts the tubes that pierce the surface, a volume integral of a 3-form counts the cells enclosed. Accepting this view explains the Jacobian: in new coordinates the integration cells must still tile the region, and the determinant that guarantees this is exactly what the wedge product generates. Example 38.1 expands the wedge of two transformed basis 1-forms and finds the 2x2 Jacobian; a margin note writes the general determinant as a Levi-Civita sum.
key_moves: Assign to each form degree a geometric picture and to each integral a counting rule (eqns 38.13-38.15).
Recall that a coordinate change requires a Jacobian so that the new cells cover the region without gaps (eqns 38.16-38.17).
Write each old basis 1-form as a linear combination of new ones via the chain rule (eqn 38.19).
Wedge them together: squares vanish, the cross terms combine with a relative minus sign by antisymmetry, and the coefficient is the determinant (eqn 38.20).

sections.title: Anatomy of an integral
sections.summary: Dissects a general multiple integral over a parametrized region into an integrand and a domain. The integrand, function times the product of differentials, is an n-form; Example 38.2 shows the flat-spacetime volume 4-form (restricted versus unrestricted sums with 1/4!), the 3-forms dSigma_mu dual to basis vectors, and the flux 3-form J^mu dSigma_mu. The domain is built locally as a wedge of the tangent vectors dP/dlambda^i scaled by parameter steps, an infinitesimal n-parallelepiped. The integral is then defined as the parameter integral of the pairing between the form and that wedge; pairing a wedge of coordinate 1-forms with the tangent wedge gives the Jacobian of coordinates with respect to parameters, so eqn 38.21 is recovered. Example 38.3 checks the definition on the integral of df along a curve, and margin notes preview the flux of a 2-form F through a small coordinate square, used in Chapter 43, and note that integrals of exact 1-forms are path independent. Conclusion: domains are dual to forms.
concepts: integral as pairing of a form with tangent n-vectors
inner product of a p-form and a p-vector
path independence of integrals of exact 1-forms
key_moves: Write the general integral with an explicit Jacobian of x with respect to lambda (eqn 38.21) and split it into four claims: integrand is an n-form, domain is an n-vector, pairing reproduces the integrand with Jacobian, geometrically the integral counts cells inside the parallelepiped.
Express the volume 4-form as (1/4!) epsilon_{mu nu alpha beta} dx^mu ^ dx^nu ^ dx^alpha ^ dx^beta and collapse it to dt^dx^dy^dz (eqn 38.23).
Build dSigma_mu = (1/3!) epsilon_{mu alpha beta gamma} dx^alpha ^ dx^beta ^ dx^gamma and contract with J^mu (eqns 38.24-38.25).
Displace a point along each parameter direction, wedge the tangent vectors, and pull the parameter steps outside (eqn 38.27).
Define the integral as the iterated parameter integral of the pairing (eqn 38.30).
Show the pairing of dx^1^...^dx^n with the tangent wedge equals the Jacobian determinant (eqn 38.32).
Test on the integral of df: the pairing gives df/dlambda and the integral gives f at the end minus f at the start (eqn 38.33).

sections.title: Boundaries and chains
sections.summary: Defines the boundary of a region as its non-interior points and treats the boundary operator as a machine: a disc gives a circle, a finite cylinder two circles, a curve its two end points, a sphere nothing (Example 38.4, Fig. 38.1). The integration domains are named chains, from 0-chains (points) to n-chains (n-volumes); a margin note mentions their origin as formal combinations of simplices in algebraic topology but says they can be thought of simply as spaces. The boundary operator lowers dimension by one. Chains with no boundary are cycles; chains that bound something are boundaries; every boundary is itself boundary-free, so applying the operator twice always gives zero. A margin note asks whether every cycle bounds and answers in terms of simple connectedness.
concepts: boundary of a boundary is zero
key_moves: Define the boundary as the set of non-interior points and give four concrete cases.
List chains by dimension (eqn 38.34) and write the boundary operator as dimension-lowering (eqn 38.35).
Name cycles (no boundary) and boundaries (B_n is the boundary of some C_{n+1}) (eqn 38.36).
Observe that a boundary has no boundary (eqn 38.37) and, since C_{n+1} was arbitrary, conclude the operator squares to zero (eqn 38.38).

sections.title: Stokes' theorem
sections.summary: Brings back the exterior derivative as the degree-raising counterpart of the boundary operator. Example 38.5 applies d to a general 1-form and 2-form in three dimensions, producing curl-like and divergence-like coefficients, and checks that a second d gives zero; dd = 0 is presented as the dual of the double-boundary rule, with closed and exact forms and the Poincaré lemma in a margin note. Stokes' theorem is then stated: for an n-form Omega and an (n+1)-chain C, integrating Omega over the boundary equals integrating dOmega over C, with the boundary oriented by dropping the first (outward) tangent direction. No proof is given. Examples 38.6 and 38.7 build the metric volume integral with sqrt(g) and a surface integral from a 2-form that yields the unit normal dotted into the area element; Example 38.8, with Fig. 38.2, recovers the endpoint theorem for a curve, the surface-to-edge theorem, the volume-to-surface theorem, and in detail the divergence theorem. The section closes by pointing to charge conservation and curvature constraints in Part VI.
concepts: duality between d and the boundary operator
key_moves: Note the parallel: boundary maps (n+1)-chains to n-chains, d maps n-forms to (n+1)-forms.
Compute dY for Y = A dx + B dy + C dz, reorder wedges and collect curl components (eqn 38.40); compute dX for a 2-form and get a divergence (eqn 38.41).
State dd = 0 (eqn 38.42) and call it dual to the double-boundary rule.
State Stokes' theorem (eqn 38.43) with the orientation convention (eqns 38.44-38.45).
Insert box vectors dx e_x, dy e_y, dz e_z into sqrt(g) dx^dy^dz to get the invariant volume element (eqns 38.46-38.47).
Fill the volume 3-form with two surface vectors and the unit normal to get a 2-form area element (eqns 38.48-38.50).
Apply Stokes to f, f dx^i and f dx^i^dx^j for the three geometries of Fig. 38.2 (eqns 38.51-38.53).
Take the flux 2-form A_x dy^dz + A_y dz^dx + A_z dx^dy, apply d, and read off the divergence theorem (eqns 38.54-38.57).

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Four bullet points: integrals are pairings of n-forms with the n-vectors representing their domains; domains are chains whose edges come from the boundary operator; the double-boundary rule says boundaries of boundaries vanish; and Stokes' theorem is restated (eqn 38.58).
concepts: boundary of a boundary is zero
key_moves: Restate the chapter's four take-aways without new material.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Four problems that apply the theorem: derive the vector curl theorem from Stokes for a 1-form; show that exact 2-forms integrate to zero over the sphere and that x^1 dx^2^dx^3 is not exact there; show the planar vortex 1-form is closed yet not exact because the origin must be removed; and a multi-part holonomy problem in which the geodesic equation on the unit sphere in an orthonormal frame, Green's theorem and Stokes combine to show that a vector carried round a closed loop is rotated by the enclosed area, with a remark that the result matters for geometric phases in magnetism.
concepts: holonomy of parallel transport on the sphere
key_moves: Exercise 38.1: apply Stokes to A_i dx^i in flat 3D.
Exercise 38.2: use the empty boundary of S^2 to kill integrals of exact forms, then exhibit a non-zero integral.
Exercise 38.3: verify d(phi) = 0 for the vortex form while its loop integral round the origin is non-zero.
Exercise 38.4: connection coefficients on the sphere, matrix-exponential solution, Green's theorem, rotation by enclosed area.

concepts.name: fundamental theorem of calculus
concepts.definition: For a differentiable function f on [a, b], the integral of its derivative over the interval equals f(b) - f(a): only boundary values survive, the upper end counted positively and the lower end negatively.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening example of the chapter, used as the prototype whose structure (derivative inside, signed boundary values outside) every later theorem copies.
concepts.notes: Re-read at the end as the 0-form case of the generalized Stokes theorem (Examples 38.3 and 38.8).

concepts.name: telescoping-sum picture of boundary terms
concepts.definition: Approximate the integral of a derivative by a sum of differences between neighbouring sample values; every interior value appears once with each sign and cancels, leaving only the difference of the extreme values.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered to explain the plus and minus signs in the fundamental theorem; later invoked verbally for the 2D theorem (interior gradients cancel, leaving circulation round the edge).
concepts.notes: This is the discrete seed of both the boundary operator with signs and Stokes' theorem; the book does not return to it explicitly.

concepts.name: volume gradient theorem
aliases: integral of a gradient over a volume
concepts.definition: The volume integral of the gradient of a scalar equals the integral of the scalar times the outward vector surface element over the closed bounding surface; componentwise, the integral of the partial derivative of f equals the integral of f dS^i.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the 3D generalization of the fundamental theorem; the sign flip of the 1D case is carried by the reversal of the outward normal on opposite faces.

concepts.name: divergence theorem
concepts.definition: For a vector field on a region V with closed boundary surface, the volume integral of its divergence equals the outward flux through the boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: First obtained from the volume gradient theorem by setting f equal to each component and summing; later re-derived in Example 38.8 by applying d to the flux 2-form A_x dy^dz + A_y dz^dx + A_z dx^dy.

concepts.name: Kelvin-Stokes theorem
concepts.definition: For a vector field and an oriented surface S bounded by a closed curve, the flux of the curl through S equals the circulation of the field round the boundary, with the curve orientation fixed by the right-hand rule.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached from an intermediate identity (area integral of gradient cross area element equals minus the loop integral of f) by taking components with the Levi-Civita symbol and contracting; set as Exercise 38.1 to rederive from the generalized theorem using a 1-form.
formulas: \int_S (\vec\nabla\times\vec a)\cdot d\vec S = \oint_{\partial S}\vec a\cdot d\vec\ell

concepts.name: differential form as integrand
concepts.definition: A p-form is a totally antisymmetric tensor that takes p vectors and returns a number; as an integrand, the function and the product of coordinate differentials together make up one form such as f dx^1 ^ ... ^ dx^p.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by rewriting work and flux integrals: the combination F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz is recognised as a 1-form and the flux combination as a 2-form, and the absence of a separate differential in the integral is defended.
concepts.notes: Forms were introduced in GA ch32; the new point here is that they are the natural thing to integrate.

concepts.name: wedge product
concepts.definition: Antisymmetric product of forms (or of vectors): a ^ b = -b ^ a for 1-forms, so any repeated factor gives zero; wedges of basis 1-forms build basis p-forms, wedges of vectors build p-vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied on throughout: to write area elements as dy^dz etc., to generate the Jacobian, and to assemble tangent parallelepipeds.
formulas: \mathbf d x\wedge\mathbf d y = -\mathbf d y\wedge\mathbf d x

concepts.name: line integral as integral of a 1-form
concepts.definition: The integral of F . dr along a curve C is the integral over C of the 1-form F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz; the form contains the differentials.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the first notational upgrade, using the work done by a force in Cartesian coordinates.
formulas: \int_C \boldsymbol F\cdot d\boldsymbol r = \int_C \tilde\alpha,\quad \tilde\alpha = F_x\mathbf dx+F_y\mathbf dy+F_z\mathbf dz

concepts.name: flux integral as integral of a 2-form
concepts.definition: The flux integral of G . dS over a surface is the integral of the 2-form G_x dy^dz + G_y dz^dx + G_z dx^dy, whose components are the Hodge-dual assignment of the vector G to oriented coordinate planes.
concepts.how_introduced: Second notational upgrade, recalling from Chapters 32 and 37 that oriented area elements are bivectors and flux is naturally a 2-form.
formulas: \int_S \boldsymbol G\cdot d\boldsymbol S = \int_S (G_x\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz + G_y\mathbf dz\wedge\mathbf dx + G_z\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy)

concepts.name: counting interpretation of form integrals
aliases: sheets crossed, tubes pierced, cells enclosed
concepts.definition: Geometrically, integrating a 1-form along a curve counts (with sign) the level sheets the curve crosses, integrating a 2-form over a surface counts the tubes that pass through it, and integrating a 3-form over a volume counts the cells it contains.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the start of Section 38.2 by recalling the pictures of forms of each degree from Chapter 32.
concepts.notes: The counts are signed and fractional in general; orientation decides the sign.

concepts.name: Jacobian determinant
concepts.definition: For a change of coordinates, the determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of one set with respect to the other; it rescales the product of differentials so that new-coordinate cells tile the region exactly.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a puzzle from ordinary multiple integration (why is there an extra factor?), then explained by the algebra of forms.
formulas: J = \varepsilon_{i_0 i_1\dots i_n}\frac{\partial x^{i_0}}{\partial y^0}\cdots\frac{\partial x^{i_n}}{\partial y^n}

concepts.name: Jacobian from wedge-product antisymmetry
concepts.definition: Substituting the chain-rule expansion of each old basis 1-form into their wedge product, and using that wedges of a 1-form with itself vanish and that swapping factors flips the sign, leaves the determinant of partial derivatives times the new basis wedge.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 38.1 in two dimensions; generalized by the pairing formula of Section 38.3.

concepts.name: Levi-Civita symbol
concepts.definition: The totally antisymmetric symbol with epsilon_{0123} = +1 (or epsilon_{12...n} = 1) and value plus or minus one for even or odd permutations, zero if any index repeats; it builds determinants and volume forms.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to express the Jacobian as a sum and the volume 4-form and 3-forms dSigma_mu.

concepts.name: volume form
concepts.definition: The top-degree form that assigns to an ordered set of n vectors the signed volume of their parallelepiped; in flat spacetime with Cartesian coordinates it is dt^dx^dy^dz, and in general coordinates it carries a factor sqrt of the absolute metric determinant. It is the Hodge dual of the constant function 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 38.2 from Chapter 37 as the integrand for 4-volume integrals; Example 38.6 builds the 3D version with sqrt(g) by feeding it coordinate box edges.
formulas: \tilde\omega = \tfrac{1}{4!}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}\,\mathbf dx^\mu\wedge\mathbf dx^\nu\wedge\mathbf dx^\alpha\wedge\mathbf dx^\beta = \mathbf dt\wedge\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz

concepts.name: hypersurface 3-form dSigma_mu
concepts.definition: In 4D, the 3-form obtained by contracting the volume form with a basis vector, (1/3!) epsilon_{mu alpha beta gamma} dx^alpha ^ dx^beta ^ dx^gamma; it is the Hodge dual of e_mu and measures oriented 3-volume of hypersurface elements.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 38.2 alongside the volume 4-form; a margin note links it to the 3-volume 1-form of Chapter 37.

concepts.name: flux 3-form J^mu dSigma_mu
concepts.definition: The 3-form obtained by contracting a 4-vector current with dSigma_mu; integrating it over a 3D hypersurface gives the flux of the current through that hypersurface (for example total charge on a spacelike slice).
concepts.how_introduced: Flagged in Example 38.2 as the kind of object that will be integrated in many applications, preparing charge conservation in Chapter 43.

concepts.name: parametrized surface
concepts.definition: An n-dimensional region described by a map from parameters (lambda^1, ..., lambda^n) to points P; the partial derivatives dP/dlambda^i are tangent vectors, and small parameter steps span an infinitesimal parallelepiped.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Section 38.3 to build the domain side of the integral; also used to state the orientation rule for the boundary.

concepts.name: p-vector
concepts.definition: A totally antisymmetric contravariant tensor built from wedges of vectors; a simple p-vector u_1 ^ ... ^ u_p represents an oriented p-dimensional parallelepiped.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled to represent the infinitesimal piece of the integration domain.

concepts.name: inner product of a p-form and a p-vector
aliases: contraction of a form with a multivector
concepts.definition: The number obtained by contracting a p-form with a p-vector using ordered (restricted) index sums; for simple p-vectors it equals the form evaluated on the constituent vectors, and geometrically it counts the form's cells inside the parallelepiped.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the 'machine' that combines integrand and domain; margin note gives the restricted-index rule and the 2-form-on-bivector case.
formulas: \langle\tilde F,\boldsymbol u\wedge\boldsymbol v\rangle = \tilde F(\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v)

concepts.name: integral as pairing of a form with tangent n-vectors
concepts.definition: The integral of an n-form over an n-dimensional parametrized region is the ordinary n-fold integral over the parameters of the pairing between the form and the wedge of tangent vectors dP/dlambda^1 ^ ... ^ dP/dlambda^n; for a coordinate n-form the pairing is the Jacobian of coordinates with respect to parameters.
concepts.how_introduced: Built step by step in Section 38.3: integrand as form, domain as wedge of tangent vectors, pairing as the multiplier; checked on the integral of df along a curve.
prerequisites: inner product of a p-form and a p-vector
concepts.notes: This is the pullback of the form to parameter space, though the book never uses the word.

concepts.name: path independence of integrals of exact 1-forms
concepts.definition: If a 1-form is the exterior derivative of a function, its integral along any curve depends only on the end points and equals the change in the function; equivalently its integral round any closed loop vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note to Example 38.3, connecting the integral of df with conservative forces.
prerequisites: integral as pairing of a form with tangent n-vectors

concepts.name: duality between forms and chains
concepts.definition: Integration pairs a p-form with a p-chain to give a number, linearly in each, in the same way a 1-form pairs with a vector; chains are the objects forms are evaluated on.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced as a slogan in Section 38.1, justified in Section 38.3 by the pairing definition of the integral, and used to motivate the boundary operator as the chain-side partner of d.
prerequisites: integral as pairing of a form with tangent n-vectors

concepts.name: boundary of a region
concepts.definition: The boundary of a region consists of its points that are not interior points; for manifolds with boundary it is the lower-dimensional edge, e.g. a disc's circle, a segment's end points.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the first definition of Section 38.4 with four quick examples (disc, cylinder, line, sphere).
concepts.notes: The set-theoretic phrasing is loose: a circle regarded as a subset of the plane has itself as its topological boundary, while as a 1-manifold it has none. The examples use the manifold sense.

concepts.name: boundary operator
concepts.definition: The operator that sends an n-chain to its (n-1)-dimensional oriented boundary; it is linear on chains and its square is zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Treated as a machine that extracts edges, illustrated pictorially in Fig. 38.1 and then made dimension-lowering on chains.
concepts.notes: The book's equation means 'is an (n-1)-chain', not equality of two specific chains; orientation signs of the boundary pieces are not discussed.

concepts.name: chain
concepts.definition: An n-chain is an n-dimensional region over which an n-form can be integrated: points (0), curves (1), surfaces (2), volumes (3) and so on; formally a combination with integer coefficients of oriented simplices, so that orientations and multiplicities are tracked.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in Section 38.1 as the dual of forms and listed by dimension in Section 38.4; a margin note mentions algebraic topology and simplicial complexes but says to picture chains as spaces.

concepts.name: cycle
concepts.definition: A chain whose boundary is zero, such as a circle or a sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Section 38.4 as the boundary-free chains; a margin note asks whether all cycles are boundaries.

concepts.name: boundary chain
concepts.definition: An n-chain that is the boundary of some (n+1)-chain, such as a closed surface bounding a volume.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with cycles; the observation that every boundary is a cycle leads to the double-boundary rule.

concepts.name: boundary of a boundary is zero
concepts.definition: Applying the boundary operator twice to any chain gives the zero chain: an edge has no edge.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by combining 'boundaries are chains of the form dC' with 'boundaries have no boundary'; drawn as the last line of Fig. 38.1.
concepts.notes: The book's derivation is essentially a restatement; the real reason is sign cancellation of shared faces (e.g. the boundary of the boundary of a triangle: each vertex appears once with plus and once with minus).

concepts.name: simply connected space
concepts.definition: A path-connected space in which every closed loop can be continuously shrunk to a point, so any two paths with the same end points can be deformed into each other.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin notes use it to answer whether cycles are boundaries and whether closed forms are exact; Exercise 38.3 shows how removing a point breaks it.
concepts.notes: Simple connectivity only settles the question for loops and 1-forms; for higher degrees one needs vanishing higher cohomology (e.g. a contractible or star-shaped region).

concepts.name: exterior derivative
concepts.definition: The linear operator that sends a p-form to a (p+1)-form, acting on functions as the gradient 1-form and satisfying a graded Leibniz rule and dd = 0; in 3D it reproduces gradient, curl and divergence on 0-, 1- and 2-forms.
concepts.how_introduced: Brought back in Section 38.5 as the counterpart of the boundary operator; Example 38.5 recomputes it on general 1- and 2-forms in three dimensions.
formulas: \mathbf d\tilde Y = \left(\partial_yC-\partial_zB\right)\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz+\left(\partial_zA-\partial_xC\right)\mathbf dz\wedge\mathbf dx+\left(\partial_xB-\partial_yA\right)\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy

concepts.name: nilpotency of the exterior derivative
concepts.definition: Applying the exterior derivative twice to any form gives zero, because mixed partial derivatives are symmetric while wedge products are antisymmetric; in 3D it contains curl grad = 0 and div curl = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Checked on the 1-form and 2-form of Example 38.5, recalled from Chapter 33, and called the dual of the double-boundary rule.

concepts.name: duality between d and the boundary operator
concepts.definition: Under the integration pairing, the exterior derivative on forms and the boundary operator on chains are adjoint: pairing dOmega with C equals pairing Omega with the boundary of C. Degree up on one side matches dimension down on the other, and dd = 0 corresponds to the double-boundary rule.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in words when d is reintroduced and when dd = 0 is called the dual of the double-boundary rule; Stokes' theorem is the precise statement.

concepts.name: closed form
concepts.definition: A form whose exterior derivative vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in a margin note to Section 38.5; the vortex form of Exercise 38.3 is the worked illustration.

concepts.name: exact form
concepts.definition: A p-form that equals the exterior derivative of some (p-1)-form; every exact form is closed because dd = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in the same margin note; Exercise 38.2 shows exact 2-forms integrate to zero over a sphere, Exercise 38.3 a closed form that fails to be exact.

concepts.name: Poincaré lemma
concepts.definition: On a contractible (for instance star-shaped) region, every closed p-form with p >= 1 is exact. For 1-forms, simple connectivity of the region is already enough.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in a margin note (stated there for simply connected regions) and tested by the vortex form on the punctured plane in Exercise 38.3.
concepts.notes: The book's margin statement with 'simply connected' is too weak for p >= 2: the solid-angle 2-form on 3D space minus the origin is closed, the domain is simply connected, but the form is not exact.

concepts.name: generalized Stokes theorem
concepts.definition: For an n-form Omega and an oriented (n+1)-chain C, the integral of dOmega over C equals the integral of Omega over the boundary of C with its induced orientation.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced as the goal in Section 38.1, motivated by the family of vector-calculus theorems, stated in Section 38.5 once forms, chains, d and the boundary operator are in hand, and exercised by recovering the classical theorems; no proof.
prerequisites: integral as pairing of a form with tangent n-vectors
concepts.notes: Metric-free: no sqrt(g) is needed in the theorem itself; metric factors enter only when converting forms into vector-calculus language.

concepts.name: induced boundary orientation
concepts.definition: If the region is oriented by the ordered tangent vectors (v_1, v_2, ..., v_n) with v_1 pointing outward at the boundary, the boundary is oriented by (v_2, ..., v_n); in 1D this gives the plus sign at the end point and minus at the start.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with Stokes' theorem via the wedge of parameter derivatives with the first one removed; a margin note glosses it as choosing a consistent positive sense pointing away from the region.
concepts.notes: The book leaves implicit that lambda^1 must be the outward direction; it also labels an (n+1)-chain with only n parameters.

concepts.name: metric volume element
concepts.definition: In a coordinate basis the volume form is sqrt(|det g|) dx^1 ^ ... ^ dx^n (with a (-1)^s sign inside the root for s minus signs in the signature); feeding it the coordinate box edges gives the scalar volume element used in integrals of functions.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 38.6 as a warm-up; margin notes recall the signature factor and that sqrt(g) returns in curved space or curvilinear coordinates.
formulas: dV = \tilde\omega(dx\,\boldsymbol e_x, dy\,\boldsymbol e_y, dz\,\boldsymbol e_z) = \sqrt g\,dx\,dy\,dz

concepts.name: surface area 2-form
aliases: area element from the volume form and unit normal
concepts.definition: In flat 3D, inserting a unit normal into the volume 3-form leaves the 2-form n^x dy^dz + n^y dz^dx + n^z dx^dy, which on two tangent vectors du, dv gives n . (du x dv), the scalar area of their parallelogram.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 38.7, used to integrate a scalar function over a surface.
formulas: \tilde\Sigma = \hat n^x\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz + \hat n^y\mathbf dz\wedge\mathbf dx+\hat n^z\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy
concepts.notes: This is the interior product of the unit normal with the volume form; it differs from the flux 2-form, where the vector field replaces the unit normal.

concepts.name: Green's theorem in the plane
concepts.definition: For functions L(x, y) and M(x, y) and a planar region S bounded by a counterclockwise curve, the circulation of L dx + M dy round the curve equals the area integral of dM/dx - dL/dy.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 38.4(b), to be verified from the generalized theorem and then applied on the sphere.

concepts.name: vortex 1-form
concepts.definition: The planar 1-form A(-y dx + x dy)/r^2, which is closed away from the origin but not exact there; its integral once round the origin is 2 pi A, which no single-valued function could produce.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 38.3, with commentary that the singular origin must be removed so the plane is no longer simply connected and the Poincaré lemma does not apply.
concepts.notes: Locally it is A d(theta) with theta the polar angle, which is multivalued; the loop value 2 pi A is our own computation.

concepts.name: holonomy of parallel transport on the sphere
concepts.definition: On the unit sphere, a tangent vector parallel transported round a closed loop returns rotated by an angle equal to the enclosed area (modulo 2 pi); on a sphere of radius R the angle is area divided by R^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 38.4, built from the orthonormal-frame geodesic equation, a matrix-exponential solution, Green's theorem and Stokes; the authors credit Blennow and Ohlsson and mention geometric phases in magnetism.
concepts.notes: A 2D instance of curvature as holonomy (GA ch11 and ch35 treat the general case).

key_equations.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
key_equations.meaning: Integrating a derivative over an interval gives the signed end values only.
key_equations.symbols: f: function; a, b: end points

key_equations.name: Telescoping sum
key_equations.meaning: Discretized version in which interior values cancel pairwise, leaving f(x_N) - f(x_1).
key_equations.symbols: Delta x: slice width; x_i: sample points, x_1 = a, x_N = b

key_equations.name: Volume gradient theorem
key_equations.latex: \int\vec\nabla f\,dV = \int f\,d\vec S\qquad\left(\int\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}dV = \int f\,dS^i\right)
key_equations.meaning: 3D analogue of the fundamental theorem; the outward surface vector supplies the sign flip. Component form from margin note 1.
key_equations.symbols: dV: volume element; dS: outward vector surface element over the closed boundary

key_equations.name: Divergence theorem
key_equations.meaning: Obtained from (38.3) by setting f = a^j and summing over j.

key_equations.name: Surface gradient identity
key_equations.meaning: 2D analogue: gradients inside a surface cancel, leaving a loop term around the edge.
key_equations.symbols: dS: vector area element; dl: line element of the bounding contour

key_equations.name: Kelvin-Stokes (curl) theorem
key_equations.meaning: Obtained from (38.5) by setting f = a^j and contracting the free index i with j.

key_equations.name: Generalized Stokes theorem (announced)
key_equations.meaning: Target of the chapter, stated before the machinery is built.
key_equations.symbols: Omega: n-form; C: (n+1)-chain; partial C: its boundary; d: exterior derivative

key_equations.name: Work integral
key_equations.meaning: A typical line integral in Cartesian coordinates.

key_equations.name: Line integral of a 1-form
key_equations.meaning: The same integral written as the integral of a 1-form with no separate differential.

key_equations.name: Flux integral with wedges
key_equations.latex: I_2 = \int_S\boldsymbol G\cdot d\boldsymbol S = \int_S(G_x\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz+G_y\mathbf dz\wedge\mathbf dx+G_z\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy)
key_equations.meaning: Surface integral with oriented area elements recast as wedges of basis 1-forms.

key_equations.name: Surface integral of a 2-form
key_equations.meaning: Flux integral as the integral of the 2-form beta = G_x dy^dz + G_y dz^dx + G_z dx^dy.

key_equations.name: Form-chain pairing slogan
key_equations.meaning: Integrands and domains are dual; putting them together gives a number, like a 1-form eating a vector.

key_equations.name: Counting rules for integrals of forms
key_equations.latex: \int_{\rm line}\tilde Y = \#\,\text{surfaces cut},\quad\int_{\rm surface}\tilde X = \#\,\text{tubes cut},\quad\int_{\rm volume}\tilde W = \#\,\text{cells contained}
key_equations.meaning: Geometric meaning of integrating 1-, 2- and 3-forms.

key_equations.name: Cartesian volume integral
key_equations.meaning: Standard multiple integral as a sum over a Cartesian cell mesh.

key_equations.name: Jacobian determinant
key_equations.latex: J = \frac{\partial(x^0,\dots,x^n)}{\partial(y^0,\dots,y^n)} = \begin{vmatrix}\partial x^0/\partial y^0&\cdots&\partial x^0/\partial y^n\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \partial x^n/\partial y^0&\cdots&\partial x^n/\partial y^n\end{vmatrix}
key_equations.meaning: Factor needed so that cells of new coordinates tile the region without gaps.

key_equations.name: Jacobian as epsilon sum
key_equations.latex: J = \varepsilon_{i_0 i_1\dots i_n}\frac{\partial x^{i_0}}{\partial y^0}\frac{\partial x^{i_1}}{\partial y^1}\cdots\frac{\partial x^{i_n}}{\partial y^n}
key_equations.meaning: Margin note: determinant written with the antisymmetric symbol, anticipating its appearance from wedges.

key_equations.name: Chain rule for basis 1-forms
key_equations.latex: \mathbf d\alpha^1 = \frac{\partial\alpha^1}{\partial x^1}\mathbf dx^1+\frac{\partial\alpha^1}{\partial x^2}\mathbf dx^2,\qquad \mathbf d\alpha^2 = \frac{\partial\alpha^2}{\partial x^1}\mathbf dx^1+\frac{\partial\alpha^2}{\partial x^2}\mathbf dx^2
key_equations.meaning: Old basis 1-forms expanded in new ones (Example 38.1).
key_equations.symbols: alpha^i: old coordinates; x^i: new coordinates

key_equations.name: Jacobian from the wedge product
key_equations.latex: \mathbf d\alpha^1\wedge\mathbf d\alpha^2 = \left(\frac{\partial\alpha^1}{\partial x^1}\frac{\partial\alpha^2}{\partial x^2}-\frac{\partial\alpha^1}{\partial x^2}\frac{\partial\alpha^2}{\partial x^1}\right)\mathbf dx^1\wedge\mathbf dx^2 = \varepsilon_{\mu\nu}\frac{\partial\alpha^\mu}{\partial x^1}\frac{\partial\alpha^\nu}{\partial x^2}\mathbf dx^1\wedge\mathbf dx^2 = \frac{\partial(\alpha^1,\alpha^2)}{\partial(x^1,x^2)}\mathbf dx^1\wedge\mathbf dx^2
key_equations.meaning: Antisymmetry of the wedge produces the determinant automatically.

key_equations.name: General multiple integral with Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: Integral of f over a region parametrized by lambda; the Jacobian meshes coordinate cells with the parametrization.
key_equations.symbols: S: region; lambda^i: parameters; coordinates now labelled from 1

key_equations.name: Integrand as an n-form
key_equations.meaning: The integrand splits into a function and a coordinate volume form.

key_equations.meaning: The current contracted into the 3-volume form; what gets integrated to count charge through a hypersurface.

key_equations.name: Integral of an n-form over an n-surface
key_equations.meaning: Generic form of the integral to be dissected.

key_equations.meaning: Margin note: the contraction counts tubes of F cut by the parallelogram u^v.

key_equations.meaning: Operational definition of integrating a form: pair it with the tangent n-vector and integrate over parameters.

key_equations.name: Coordinate n-form
key_equations.meaning: Form to be inserted in the pairing (printed without the tilde).

key_equations.name: Pairing gives the Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: Why the definition (38.30) reproduces (38.21).

key_equations.name: Chains by dimension
key_equations.latex: C_0 = \text{point},\ C_1=\text{line},\ C_2=\text{area},\ C_3 = \text{3-volume},\ C_n = n\text{-volume}
key_equations.meaning: Naming of chains.

key_equations.meaning: The boundary of an n-chain is an (n-1)-chain.

key_equations.name: Boundary chains
key_equations.meaning: An n-chain that bounds some (n+1)-chain.

key_equations.name: Boundaries are closed
key_equations.meaning: A boundary has no boundary.

key_equations.meaning: The boundary operator squares to zero.

key_equations.meaning: General 0-, 1-, 2-, 3-forms used in Example 38.5.

key_equations.latex: \mathbf d\tilde Y = \left(\frac{\partial C}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial B}{\partial z}\right)\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz+\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}\right)\mathbf dz\wedge\mathbf dx+\left(\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial A}{\partial y}\right)\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy
key_equations.meaning: Coefficients are the curl components of (A, B, C).

key_equations.name: Exterior derivative of a 2-form in 3D
key_equations.latex: \mathbf d\tilde X = \left(\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial b}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}\right)\mathbf dx\wedge\mathbf dy\wedge\mathbf dz
key_equations.meaning: A divergence; note a multiplies dx^dy so it pairs with d/dz.

key_equations.name: Nilpotency of d
key_equations.meaning: Two exterior derivatives give zero; dual to (38.38).

key_equations.name: Stokes' theorem
key_equations.meaning: For an n-form and an (n+1)-chain, the boundary integral of the form equals the region integral of its exterior derivative.

key_equations.name: Induced boundary orientation
key_equations.meaning: Drop the first tangent direction (implicitly the outward one) to orient the boundary.

key_equations.name: Metric volume 3-form
key_equations.meaning: Volume 3-form in a coordinate frame of 3D space, shown with three empty slots to be filled by edge vectors.
